questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a persuasive text?
options: To convince the reader of a point of view
questions.explanation: Persuasion aims to change what the reader thinks or does.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of an informative text?
options: To give the reader factual information
questions.explanation: Information texts explain or report rather than argue.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a procedure text?
options: To tell the reader how to do something in steps
questions.explanation: Recipes and instruction manuals are procedures.

questions.stem: What is an audience in writing?
options: The people the text is written for
The people who appear in the text
questions.explanation: Audience shapes vocabulary, tone and structure.

questions.stem: What is a topic sentence?
options: A sentence stating the main idea of a paragraph
The last sentence of a paragraph
questions.explanation: Topic sentences usually open a paragraph and signal what it will cover.
questions.teaching:
Paragraphs in non-fiction usually have a structure, and there is a standard name for the sentence that announces what the paragraph is about.

It normally sits at the start, states the main idea in general terms, and the rest of the paragraph then supports it with evidence, examples and explanation. Every paragraph can have one, which is why it is not the same as the opening line of the whole text. The practical use is in skimming: read only these across a long article and you get its argument. Writing them well is also the fastest way to make an essay easier to follow.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a heading in an informative text?
options: To signal what a section is about so readers can navigate
To make the page look attractive only
questions.explanation: Headings are a structural signal — one of the cohesion devices that tells a reader how a text is organised.

questions.stem: What is a fact?
options: A statement that can be checked and verified
questions.explanation: Facts are verifiable. Opinions express a view.
questions.teaching:
Distinguishing between two kinds of statement is a foundation skill for evaluating any source.

One kind can be checked against evidence and settled — a date, a measurement, a documented event. It can be right or wrong, but the point is that a method exists for finding out. The other kind expresses a judgement, preference or belief, and cannot be settled the same way. Both belong in good writing; the trouble comes when one is presented as the other, which is a standard persuasive move.

questions.stem: What is an opinion?
options: A statement expressing a personal view or judgement
A statement that can be proven
questions.explanation: Opinions can be supported with evidence but are not themselves verifiable.

questions.stem: What is inference in reading?
options: Copying a sentence from the text
Working out something the text implies but does not state directly
questions.explanation: Inference combines textual clues with what you already know.

questions.stem: What is summarising?
options: Writing your opinion of the text
Restating the main ideas briefly in your own words
questions.explanation: A summary keeps the main ideas and drops the detail.

questions.stem: What is a chronological text structure?
options: Ideas organised by cause and effect
questions.explanation: Chronology follows the sequence of events, as in a biography or recount.

questions.stem: What is a cause and effect text structure?
options: Showing how one event leads to another
questions.explanation: Cause and effect explains why something happened, not just when.

questions.stem: What is a taxonomy in a text?
options: A classification of things into groups and subgroups
questions.explanation: Taxonomies organise ideas hierarchically — a structure the curriculum names explicitly.

questions.stem: Which word signals a contrast?
questions.explanation: 'However' signals contrast; 'furthermore' adds, 'similarly' compares and 'therefore' concludes.
questions.teaching:
Connectives signal the relationship between one idea and the next, and they come in families according to what they signal.

Some add — also, furthermore, in addition. Some sequence — first, next, finally. Some show cause — therefore, as a result, consequently. Some give examples. And one family warns the reader that what follows will run against what came before. Choosing a connective from the wrong family actively misleads, so matching signal to relationship is the skill being tested.

questions.stem: Which word signals a conclusion or result?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' introduces a consequence.
questions.teaching:
Connectives are grouped by the relationship they signal, and knowing the groups makes both reading and writing easier.

One group adds information. One sequences it. One contrasts it. And one signals that what follows is the consequence of what came before — the conclusion drawn from it, or the result it produced. These are what let a reader follow an argument without re-reading, because each one tells you in advance what kind of thing is coming next.

questions.stem: What is a connective?
options: A word or phrase that links ideas between sentences or paragraphs
The main verb of a sentence
questions.explanation: Connectives such as 'in addition' and 'as a result' create cohesion.

questions.stem: What does 'evidence' mean in an argument?
options: Information used to support a claim
questions.explanation: Evidence substantiates a claim — statistics, examples, expert statements.
questions.teaching:
An argument has two parts: what you claim, and what you offer to make the claim believable.

The second part has to be something a reader can check independently — statistics, documented examples, quotations from the text, findings from a study, expert testimony. Restating the claim more forcefully is not it, however confident the wording. Neither is asserting that something is obvious. When analysing persuasive writing, a useful question is what would have to be true for this claim to hold, and whether the writer has shown it.

questions.stem: What is a rhetorical question?
options: A question asked by a character
A question asked for effect rather than to get an answer
A question the writer answers immediately
questions.explanation: 'Do we really want that future?' is meant to prompt agreement, not a reply.
questions.teaching:
Persuasive writers use several devices that involve questions, and this one is a question in form only.

The speaker is not seeking information and does not pause for a reply. Instead the question is framed so the audience supplies the intended answer themselves — 'how much longer can we wait?' pushes towards a conclusion far more effectively than stating it would. Because the listener does the concluding, they feel they arrived at it independently, which is precisely why speeches and editorials are full of them.

questions.stem: What is emotive language?
options: Language chosen to provoke a strong feeling in the reader
questions.explanation: Words like 'devastating' or 'heartless' push the reader towards a feeling.
questions.teaching:
Two writers can report the same event with the same facts and produce completely different effects, and word choice is usually where the difference lives.

Some wording is chosen to keep the reader neutral. Other wording is selected specifically to provoke a response — pity, anger, fear, admiration. 'Slaughtered' and 'killed' describe the same outcome; 'crowd' and 'mob' describe the same people. Spotting which choices are doing that work, and naming the feeling they aim at, is most of what analysing persuasive language actually involves.

questions.stem: Why does a recipe use short numbered steps rather than flowing paragraphs?
options: The structure matches its purpose — following actions in order while cooking
Paragraphs are grammatically wrong in recipes
questions.explanation: Structure follows purpose. A reader with their hands busy needs to find their place instantly.

questions.stem: A text uses 'firstly', 'in addition' and 'finally'. What are these doing?
options: Signalling the sequence and structure of the argument
questions.explanation: These are cohesive devices that guide the reader through the structure.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the language of evaluation?
options: The report is forty pages long.
This approach is by far the most effective solution available.
questions.explanation: Evaluation makes a judgement. The other three simply state information.

questions.stem: Which statement is substantiated?
options: Attendance rose 18% after the change, according to the school's own records.
questions.explanation: Substantiation supplies verifiable support. 'Everyone knows' and 'obviously' assert without evidence.

questions.stem: How would a text about climate change differ for scientists versus primary students?
options: Vocabulary, sentence complexity and assumed knowledge would all change
Only the images would change, not the writing
questions.explanation: Audience drives language choices, but the underlying facts should not shift.

questions.stem: A paragraph begins 'Despite these benefits...'. What does this signal?
options: A summary of the whole text
A shift to drawbacks or counter-arguments
questions.explanation: 'Despite' signals concession, warning the reader that a contrast is coming.

questions.stem: What can you infer from 'She checked the lock three times before leaving'?
options: She is anxious or does not trust the lock
questions.explanation: Repeated checking suggests anxiety. Inference draws on behaviour, not stated facts.

questions.stem: Why do persuasive texts often use statistics?
options: They appear objective and substantiate claims
They replace the need for an argument
questions.explanation: Statistics lend authority — which is also why a critical reader checks their source.

questions.stem: A news report uses 'protesters clashed with police'. What does the word 'clashed' suggest?
options: Mutual conflict, without assigning blame to either side
questions.explanation: Word choice shapes meaning even in supposedly neutral reporting.

questions.stem: How does a comparison text structure organise ideas?
options: By setting out similarities and differences between two or more things
By listing events in time order
By grouping items into a hierarchy
questions.explanation: Comparison texts move between subjects on shared criteria.

questions.stem: Why does an explanation text usually use present tense?
options: It describes how something generally works, not a one-off past event
questions.explanation: 'Water evaporates when heated' is a general truth, so present tense fits.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a counter-argument in a persuasive text?
options: To acknowledge an opposing view and then refute it, strengthening credibility
questions.explanation: Addressing objections shows the writer has considered the issue, which makes the argument harder to dismiss.

questions.stem: Why can cohesion fail even when every sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Cohesion follows automatically from correct punctuation
Without signals linking ideas, the reader cannot see how the sentences relate
Cohesion depends on sentence length rather than linking
Cohesion is judged within each sentence separately
questions.explanation: Cohesion operates between sentences. A list of correct but unconnected statements is hard to follow.

questions.stem: A writer says 'studies show' but names no study. What is the weakness?
options: The claim appears substantiated but cannot be checked
The phrase should be 'research shows' instead
questions.explanation: Unattributed appeals borrow the appearance of evidence without its substance.

questions.stem: How does the structure of a taxonomy help a reader understand a complex topic?
options: It puts ideas in time order
It groups related ideas so relationships and levels are visible at a glance
It removes the need for examples
questions.explanation: Hierarchy carries information: what belongs with what, and what sits under what.

questions.stem: Two texts present the same statistics but reach opposite conclusions. What best explains this?
options: They select, frame and interpret the data differently
One text has invented its figures
The conclusions must be identical really
questions.explanation: Framing and selection do enormous work. This is why identifying what a text leaves out matters as much as what it includes.

questions.stem: Why is inference described as a strategy rather than a guess?
options: It is another word for summarising
It is reasoned from evidence in the text combined with prior knowledge
questions.explanation: A good inference can be justified by pointing to what in the text supports it.

questions.stem: A writer moves from chronological to cause-and-effect structure midway. What might justify this?
options: Chronology cannot be combined with any other structure
The purpose shifts from recounting what happened to explaining why
questions.explanation: Structure follows purpose, so a shift in purpose can warrant a shift in structure — provided it is signalled clearly.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evaluation of a persuasive text?
options: It identifies the claim, examines the evidence, and judges whether the evidence supports it
It states whether the reader agreed
It counts the persuasive devices used
questions.explanation: Evaluation requires judgement grounded in the relationship between claim and evidence, not just device-spotting or personal reaction.

questions.stem: What is a bias in a text?
options: A leaning towards one point of view
questions.explanation: Bias can appear through word choice, selection of facts and omission.
questions.teaching:
Bias is not the same as inaccuracy, and confusing the two is what makes it hard to detect.

It is a leaning towards one side, shown through which facts are included and left out, which words are chosen, whose voices are quoted, and what is treated as obvious. Crucially, every individual statement in a biased text can be entirely true — which is why fact-checking alone will not find it. Every text has a perspective, so the useful question is what that perspective is and what it does to the reader.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a review?
options: To evaluate something and give a judgement
questions.explanation: Reviews combine description with evaluation.

questions.stem: What is a recount?
options: A retelling of events in the order they happened
questions.explanation: Recounts are chronological and usually in past tense.

questions.stem: What is skimming a text?
options: Reading quickly to get the general idea
questions.explanation: Scanning looks for specific information; skimming gets the gist.

questions.stem: What is scanning a text?
questions.explanation: You scan a timetable for one departure, rather than reading it all.

questions.stem: What is a subheading for?
options: Signalling the content of a smaller section
questions.explanation: Subheadings break a text into navigable parts.
questions.teaching:
Texts aimed at readers who will skim rather than read straight through use signposts, and each has its own job.

A heading names the whole text or a major part. Below that, smaller signposts break a long section into manageable pieces and tell a reader what each piece covers, so they can find what they need or decide to skip ahead. Together these features form the structure a reader navigates by. A caption does something different again, explaining an image rather than a block of text.

questions.stem: What is an anecdote in persuasive writing?
options: A short personal story used to illustrate a point
questions.explanation: Anecdotes engage readers emotionally but are weak as evidence on their own.
questions.teaching:
Persuasive texts use several kinds of support, and each works on the reader differently.

Statistics and expert opinion appeal to reason and carry weight through authority. A short personal story works a different way: it makes an abstract argument concrete and invites the reader to feel it rather than weigh it. That vividness is its power, and also its weakness — a single case proves very little about the general pattern, which is exactly why writers reach for one when the general pattern is not on their side. Good analysis names both the effect and the limitation.

questions.stem: What is a glossary?
options: A list of terms with their definitions
questions.explanation: Glossaries support readers with technical vocabulary.
questions.teaching:
Informative texts include navigation features that help a reader find and understand content without reading straight through.

A contents page lists sections in order. An index lists topics alphabetically with page numbers. Headings and subheadings signal what each part covers. Captions explain images. And one feature collects the specialist terms used in the text and explains them, usually at the back — which is what lets a reader who does not know a term keep going rather than stopping.

questions.stem: What does a bibliography list?
questions.explanation: Listing sources allows readers to check the evidence.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an explanation text?
options: To describe how or why something happens
questions.explanation: Explanations usually use present tense and cause-and-effect structure.

questions.stem: A text says 'nine out of ten experts agree' without naming them. What should a critical reader do?
options: Ask which experts, and how they were selected
questions.explanation: Unsourced authority claims are neither automatically true nor false — they are uncheckable, which is the problem.

questions.stem: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about recycling benefits?
options: Recycling reduces landfill and conserves raw materials.
questions.explanation: A topic sentence states the paragraph's controlling idea clearly.

questions.stem: Why do informative texts often avoid emotive language?
options: Emotive language makes a text harder to translate
The purpose is to inform rather than to sway the reader's feelings
Emotive language belongs only in spoken texts
questions.explanation: Register follows purpose, though no text is entirely neutral.

questions.stem: A writer describes a policy as 'reckless'. What is this an example of?
questions.explanation: The word carries a judgement that would need substantiating.

questions.stem: What does a writer signal with 'in contrast'?
options: A difference is about to be presented
questions.explanation: Connectives tell the reader what relationship follows.

questions.stem: Why should a summary avoid the writer's own opinion?
options: A summary reports what the text says, not what the reader thinks of it
questions.explanation: Evaluation is a separate task from summarising.

questions.stem: A text about a new stadium quotes only local businesses. What is the weakness?
options: Business quotations carry less weight than statistics
It omits perspectives such as residents or environmental groups
questions.explanation: Selection of voices shapes the picture as much as what those voices say.

questions.stem: Why does identifying a text's purpose help a reader evaluate it?
options: Purpose has no bearing on content
It tells you the author's name
Purpose explains why particular information was included or left out
questions.explanation: An advertisement and a report can describe the same product very differently, and both are doing their job.

questions.stem: Two texts on the same topic use different structures. How does this affect the reader?
options: It affects how formal the text sounds
Structure guides which relationships between ideas are foregrounded
Structure decides which text is more accurate
The reader has to reorder one text to compare them
questions.explanation: A chronological account emphasises sequence; a cause-and-effect account emphasises explanation.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a strong inference from a weak one?
options: A strong inference is more surprising
A strong inference states something the text says directly
A strong inference can be traced to specific evidence in the text
questions.explanation: The test is whether you can point to what supports it.

questions.stem: Why might a writer place their strongest argument last?
options: Because the first point is always weakest
To leave the reader with the most compelling point in mind
questions.explanation: Position affects emphasis, though some writers lead with the strongest point instead.

questions.stem: A text presents a statistic without a comparison point. Why is this a problem?
options: A number alone cannot show whether it is high, low or typical
It makes the text too short
questions.explanation: 'Crime rose by 200 cases' means little without knowing the base and the trend.

questions.stem: Why is cohesion described as operating at the level of the whole text?
options: It applies to written texts but not spoken ones
Devices such as headings, referencing and connectives link sections, not just sentences
Cohesion is created by paragraph length
Cohesion depends on using the same tense throughout
questions.explanation: Repeated key terms and consistent referencing hold a whole text together.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest response to a text you disagree with?
options: Identify its claims and evidence, then explain specifically where the reasoning fails
Summarise the text fairly, then state that your own view differs from the author's
Find the strongest counter-example you know and present it without addressing theirs
Explain how the text made you feel and why other readers would feel the same
questions.explanation: Engaging with the argument itself is what makes a critique persuasive.

questions.stem: What is a narrative text?
options: A text that tells a story
A text that argues a case
questions.explanation: Narratives have characters, setting and a sequence of events.
questions.teaching:
Texts are classified by purpose, and each type has a recognisable structure.

One type tells a story, usually with an orientation, a complication and a resolution, and characters who change. Another explains how something works. Another argues a position. Another recounts real events in order. The first type is defined by having a plot with a problem in it, which is what separates it from a recount — a recount tells you what happened, but nothing has to go wrong.

questions.stem: What is an editorial?
options: An opinion piece expressing a publication's view
questions.explanation: Editorials argue rather than simply report.

questions.stem: What is a hyperlink in a digital text?
options: A clickable link to related content
questions.explanation: Digital texts allow non-linear reading, which changes how readers navigate.
questions.teaching:
Digital texts can be navigated in ways print cannot, and this is the feature that makes that possible.

Rather than reading straight through, a reader can jump to related material by selecting something on the page — a word, an image, a menu item — and be taken elsewhere. That means digital texts are often read non-linearly, with each reader taking a different path. It also affects how you evaluate them: where a jump takes you, and who controls the destination, is worth checking.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a topic sentence in a paragraph?
options: To state the paragraph's main idea
questions.explanation: Supporting sentences then develop that idea.

questions.stem: What is a text's register?
options: Its level of formality and the style suited to its audience
questions.explanation: A text message and a job application use very different registers.

questions.stem: What is a conclusion in a persuasive text?
options: A final section restating the position and its strongest support
questions.explanation: Conclusions consolidate rather than introduce new arguments.

questions.stem: What is an infographic?
options: A visual display presenting information or data
questions.explanation: Infographics combine text and visuals to convey information quickly.

questions.stem: What is a quotation used for in an argument?
options: Providing evidence in the words of a source
questions.explanation: Quotations support a point; they do not make it on their own.

questions.stem: What does 'objective' mean when describing writing?
options: Based on facts rather than personal feelings
questions.explanation: Subjective writing foregrounds personal viewpoint.

questions.stem: What is a caption's purpose?
options: Explaining what an image shows and how it relates to the text
questions.explanation: Captions connect visual and written information.

questions.stem: A writer opens with a shocking statistic. What is the likely purpose?
options: To capture attention and establish urgency
questions.explanation: Openings are designed to engage before the argument develops.

questions.stem: Why do digital texts change how people read?
options: Digital texts are read more slowly than printed ones
Links and scrolling encourage non-linear, selective reading
Digital texts rely on images rather than words
Readers finish digital texts more often than printed ones
questions.explanation: The curriculum asks students to explain the effect of technology on reading and responding.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows substantiation rather than assertion?
options: Rates fell 12% over three years, according to the department's annual report.
Rates have clearly fallen a lot.
questions.explanation: A specific figure with a named source can be checked.

questions.stem: Why might a text present a counter-argument early?
options: To address a reader's likely objection before building its own case
questions.explanation: Pre-empting objections builds credibility with a sceptical reader.

questions.stem: How does paragraph length affect a reader?
options: Short paragraphs speed reading and emphasise; long ones develop ideas in depth
Paragraph length is set by the publisher, not the writer
questions.explanation: Structure shapes pace just as sentence length does.

questions.stem: Why can omission be as persuasive as inclusion?
options: Omission is persuasive only when the reader spots it
Leaving out inconvenient information shapes the reader's conclusion without any false statement
questions.explanation: Asking what a text leaves out is a key critical reading move.

questions.stem: How does a taxonomy differ from a simple list?
options: It shows hierarchy and relationships, not just items
questions.explanation: Nesting carries information about how ideas relate.

questions.stem: Two texts describe the same event with different structures. How does this affect meaning?
options: Structure affects tone but not what the reader concludes
Structure foregrounds different relationships, such as sequence versus causation
Structure changes only how long the text takes to read
The text using chronology will always be the more accurate
questions.explanation: How ideas are organised is itself a claim about how they relate.

questions.stem: What makes a summary difficult to write well?
options: Deciding what is essential requires understanding the whole text's argument
questions.explanation: Selection is the hard part, and it demonstrates comprehension.

questions.stem: Why is an appeal to emotion not automatically a weakness in an argument?
options: Emotion can legitimately convey stakes, provided the argument also has evidence
Emotion is required in all texts
questions.explanation: The problem is emotion substituting for evidence, not emotion accompanying it.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest way to evaluate whether a text achieved its purpose?
options: Compare it with another text on the subject and decide which of the two you preferred
Identify the purpose, then judge whether the structure and language served it for that audience
Count the persuasive devices used and judge it by how many it includes
Check whether it follows the conventions of its text type throughout
questions.explanation: Evaluation must be measured against what the text was trying to do.
